extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legal and economic analysts, and stakeholders studying Quebec sovereignty and its economic/trade/monetary implications
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for assessing whether and how a sovereign Quebec could maintain the existing Canadian market common (monetary union, free trade, regulatory harmonization, international treaty membership). Focuses on GATT accession, US free-trade relations, monetary arrangements, sectoral protections, movement of persons, and coordination mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: GATT accession: routes and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: L'accession d’un nouvel état membre au GATT peut s’effectuer de deux façons: par voie de négociations (article XXXIII) ou par voie de succession (article XXVI). Dans le cas d’une accession par succession, le territoire autonome est réputé signataire et adopte les concessions et la grille tarifaire de l’État prédécesseur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Quebec became a GATT member by succession it would presumptively adopt the Canadian tariff schedule in force at accession; however acceptance by other contracting parties is conditional on sufficient international recognition of Quebec as a sovereign state. Once admitted, Quebec’s participation in renegotiation processes and institutions would depend on any coordination arrangement with the rest of Canada. Bilateral agreements signed under the GATT (e.g., 25 textile/clothing import restriction agreements) would likely need to be renegotiated and re-signed jointly or separately. The page notes practical implications and that, in practice, accession by succession is feasible but conditioned on recognition and coordination of commercial policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation/ succession of Canada–United States free-trade agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional state practice holds that treaties tied to territory automatically apply to a successor only if territorial in character; the Canada–US Free-Trade Agreement (now NAFTA context) would not automatically succeed to Quebec. The 1978 Vienna Convention proposes automatic succession for seceding entities, but Canada has not adopted it; moreover adding a third partner changes treaty execution conditions and likely precludes automatic succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sovereign Quebec would probably need to renegotiate/free sign a free-trade agreement with the United States (either tripartite Québec–Canada–US or bilateral Québec–US). In the interim de facto application of substantive provisions could be envisaged (as at GATT), but formal acceptance requires negotiation. Political and economic factors (US interest in stability and access to Canadian resources, ongoing US trade initiatives) make US willingness to renegotiate likely; however certain contentious sectors (e.g., alcohol trade, agricultural supply-managed sectors) might lead the US to seek to leverage concessions during renegotiation. Overall, succession to the Canada–US FTA is not automatic and would require explicit arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas requiring harmonization to preserve the market common
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining the essential elements of the Canadian market common would require harmonizations in monetary policy, internal and external commercial policy, and various legislations and regulations affecting the freedom of movement of persons, goods, services and capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report identifies specific policy domains where harmonization is necessary: currency/monetary arrangements, trade policy (domestic and external), social programs and transfers (affecting mobility), regulations governing goods and services, and capital movement rules. Preservation of these elements reduces resource misallocation and transaction costs; loss of harmonization would fragment markets and raise inefficient costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for defining, applying and arbitrating harmonization measures
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain harmonization the Quebec and Canadian governments would need mechanisms to define, apply and arbitrate measures of coordination; options include a formal association treaty or sectoral agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that a general treaty of economic association (reassociation) raises complex legal, political and institutional issues; however the absence of a single general treaty does not preclude many sectoral agreements. Practical mechanisms might include negotiated sectoral accords, joint institutions or arbitration bodies; the choice affects enforceability and ease of preserving market common elements. The European experience is cited as relevant but not analyzed in detail in the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary arrangement: currency choice and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Two fundamental questions: whether to adopt a distinct Quebec currency, and how monetary policy would be determined if Quebec continued using the Canadian dollar. A distinct currency would introduce transaction costs (conversion) and exchange-rate risk; studies suggest transaction costs could be ~1% of GDP in small open economies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting a Quebec currency would impose conversion transaction costs and exchange-rate uncertainty on a small, highly integrated economy; estimates translated to Quebec imply significant annual costs (~1.6 billion 1990 dollars). For credibility, a new Quebec currency would likely need to be pegged to the Canadian or US dollar, which would limit true monetary autonomy. Independent expansionary monetary policy risks currency depreciation, higher inflation, higher interest rates and investment disincentives. The report concludes that continued use of a common currency is the best option to preserve the market common, though institutional arrangements (e.g., legal tender status, liquidity arrangements with Canadian payment associations) could be implemented with minimal gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation in central bank governance and sharing of central bank profits
rubrics_metrics.description: If Quebec continued using the Canadian dollar it could seek legal measures to keep the dollar in circulation and negotiate participation in Bank of Canada decision-making and a share of Bank of Canada profits; profit sharing relates to the broader division of federal assets and liabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping the Canadian dollar as legal tender in Quebec could be achieved by domestic legislation and liquidity arrangements via membership in Canadian payments associations. Negotiating representation in the Bank of Canada’s governance (appointments to its board) is possible but likely to yield minority influence. Quebec might also claim a share of seigniorage/profits (because the Bank holds federal government securities against currency issued), but this ties into broader negotiations over division of federal assets and liabilities and would require political negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving internal free trade: absence of tariffs, quantitative restrictions, and customs controls
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve the market common Quebec and Canada should agree to maintain the current absence of tariffs and quantitative restrictions in mutual trade and to avoid customs controls at common borders; they should renounce the unilateral right to impose tariffs/quantitative restrictions allowed under GATT by reestablishing internal free trade by agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-establishing internal free trade by mutual agreement (rather than relying on constitutional Article 121 alone) and coordination of external trade policy are important; lack of alignment would force origin checks and border controls, generating significant costs for travelers and commerce (including transit trade like Atlantic provinces’ goods through Quebec). Maintaining a common external commercial policy avoids origin verification and reduces administrative/border costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific protection and quota regimes (textiles, clothing, dairy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain industries (textiles, clothing, dairy) are significantly protected under current Canadian policy (quotas, import restrictions). These protectionist elements raise questions about whether the rest of Canada would maintain a customs union that preserves such protections for Quebec producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textiles and clothing: Canada had 25 bilateral import-restriction agreements under GATT expected to be renegotiated; Quebec is a major producer in these sectors (48% of textiles, 61% of clothing production). Dairy: supply-management quotas allocate production shares by province (Quebec producers account for ~48% of Canadian production); GATT Article XI limits some types of import restrictions by preventing import shares from falling below pre-restriction levels. The report argues that because other provinces also benefit, and because opening borders would harm multiple provinces, wholesale removal of protection is unlikely immediately; sectoral outcomes depend on negotiation and GATT rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of movement of persons and transferability of social and pension rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to establish and earn a living in any province is central to the Canadian market common; to make this effective after sovereignty Quebec and Canada would need mechanisms guaranteeing continuity of access to social programs and transferability of rights (unemployment insurance, social assistance, public pension plans, OAS, private pension portability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserving mobility requires reciprocal arrangements ensuring continuity of eligibility for major social programs and pensions when people move between Quebec and the rest of Canada. Mechanisms should include compensation systems for program entitlements and harmonization of private pension rules and relevant tax provisions, so migrants do not lose benefits or face discontinuities that would deter movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of implementing border controls and rules of origin if harmonization fails
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing customs controls and rules of origin on the Quebec–Canada border would impose significant direct costs on travelers and firms and would disrupt existing transit trade (e.g., $10 billion of interprovincial goods transiting Quebec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report highlights that border controls (air, land, sea) would impose transaction costs that argue strongly for maintaining internal free trade or a customs union. Failure to coordinate external commercial policy would necessitate origin verification at borders (as in CUSFTA/NAFTA rules of origin), greatly increasing administrative burdens and trade costs; this cost consideration is a practical criterion favoring harmonization or negotiated arrangements.
